en: This is called the Ālokamālā. Homage to the Buddha.
Homage to that Lord of Sages, by whom the state of "mind-only" was taught for the sake of destroying the three types of ignorance through the cultivation of the three natures.
2. Elaboration has been described by the Destroyer of the Three Realms as being, in brief, nothing but the conceptual construction of the mind;
if that is entirely cast out from the heart, [then all is attained].
And the connection of rebirth for eight more lifetimes has been severed.
3. Because of the thorough knowledge of existence and liberation, there arises the fruit of their abandonment and attainment;
this is the labor of study in the inner science for all who possess sound intelligence.
4. The mind defiled by passion and other stains is saṃsāra; its state of being free from those [stains] is, in brief, declared as liberation by the Victors who have abandoned all obscurations.
5. Passion, the conceptualization of one's own mind, darkness, and hatred belong to embodied beings;
so too do those other phenomena which have been falsely imagined by the ignorant who possess a false sense of self.
6. Even regarding conceptual constructions concerning the ultimate truth, the wise person should not become attached;
for what difference is there between a conceptual construction that is wholesome or even unwholesome?
7. There is no difference in fire regarding its power to burn based on the difference of its substratum;
even when ignited upon sandalwood, it certainly burns when touched.
8. Indeed, every conceptual construction (parikalpa), even that which is subtle, must be abandoned;
for conceptualization, being of the nature of delusion, leads only to a flooding of the heart.
Even delusion, due to its impurity, is a manifestation of a magical illusion;
and that magical illusion, too, should be known as nothing more than a confusion of the mind.
10. Thus, the vision of non-duality regarding that mind and its delusion is itself the Middle Way; it is itself the selflessness of phenomena.
11. That very [reality] is the limit of existence, it is suchness, it is emptiness;
it is equality, it is liberation, and it is representation-only.
12. Among all phenomena, sentient beings are neither distant nor near;
because suchness is realized without difficulty, its form is not subject to transformation.
13. But because of its subtlety, that [emptiness] is self-cognizable by the Buddhas who perceive the subtle;
it is not perceived even when residing in its own substratum by those like me, whose intellects are coarse.
14. The knower of yoga should not, under any circumstances, perceive liberation as something distant;
for when one’s own self is seen as empty of imagined form, that is nirvāṇa.
15. Illusions such as the sun, water, darkness, dreams, and cities of the Gandharvas, though they are delusions, are beneficial because they dispel other delusions.
For those whose minds are distracted by day by various conceptualizations of sense-objects,
the poison of latent impressions (vāsanā) becomes intensely turbulent even in dreams due to the force of that [distraction].
17. Oh, how dense is the continuity of false conceptualization!
It is like a pustule upon a boil, or one dream within another dream.
Ignorance, as soon as it arises, manifests an unreal object while obscuring the real,
just like the onset of jaundice.
Though undivided, the mind appears in many ways through differentiation— appearing as if external though not gone outside, and turbid with the forms of objects.
The sun and moon, the sky, the circle of stars, the earth, the rivers,
the oceans, the quarters, and the mountains— these are the manifestations of the mind.
21. This triple world, as far as its limit at the peak of existence, is all that which is proclaimed by the drops of poison from the consciousness-snake.

22. If it is said that there is no appearance because of destruction, how can there be an appearance of that which is non-existent by nature? Existence does not follow from appearance; for what is seen in a dream is not [ultimately] perceived.
23. Their own piercing clarity concealed by the stains born of their substrate, cognitions shine through the form of others, like crystals.

24. Although it is not visible by its own nature when smeared with the latent impressions of formative forces (*saṃskāra-vāsanā*), conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) attains visibility only after reaching growth over time.
25. Even a single mind appears as two due to the distortion of its forms; through some extraordinary skill, it appears as the distinction between the grasped object and the grasping subject.
26. The aspect of the apprehended, due to its lack of activity, appears as if external;
the apprehender, however, because it possesses vitality, seems to throb within.
27. Herein, there is nothing external nor internal, because they are established in mutual dependence;
there is nothing in between, nor is there non-existence at all, since everything is established as mind-only.
28. For passion resides neither in the collection of sense-faculties, nor in objects, nor in the mind;
it is not situated in another, nor is it situated in oneself; furthermore, it is neither existent nor non-existent.
29. From a mental delusion whose cause—the connection—is not clearly discerned, [a result] arises from some opening in the ocean like a thunderbolt-fire.
30. In this way, both hatred and delusion, as well as other types of afflictions that spread throughout the three realms, arise from the poison of conceptual construction.
31. Even conceptual construction, being without a basis, does not exist from the perspective of ultimate reality.
Has anyone ever seen a fire-extinguishing thunderbolt blazing in the sky?

32. The antidote as well—beginning with the meditation on the foul and so forth—has been taught by the Lord of Sages for the destruction of the poison of doubt, just as experts [use] deceptive mantras.
33. In the absence of substantiality, there is no jasmine, blue lotus, or the like, nor excrement and so forth;
it is as in the state of dreaming regarding women, while in the waking state there is the physical body.
34. Thinking thus that both passion and dispassion are false, one is neither impassioned nor dispassionate anywhere, because the closed fist has been opened.
35. For whom there is dispassion, for him there will undoubtedly be passion again.
Therefore, for the sake of abandoning passion, one should not even touch upon dispassion.
36. Oh, the solitude of this path that transcends the world!
That which is a word of truth elsewhere is here a word of falsehood.
37. Even that which is true, if spoken for the purpose of causing harm, is indeed falsehood.
What is the use of truth that is neither beneficial to oneself nor to others? That alone is truth which accomplishes the welfare of others.
38. The wise say that the knowledge of truth as truth is itself truth;
however, one who perceives truth through the lens of untruth does not abide in truth.
39. The speech of the ignorant world is better taken as truth than that which is untrue;
for since the intellects of those who must travel [through saṃsāra] are unreal, at the end, everything has that [reality] as its essence.
40. Thus, everything is false to the extent that it is conceptualized;
that which is not conceptualized is the truth, that which is as it is, the reality.
41. One who is puffed up with self-conceit does not stop at this [point];
by means of proofs and refutations, he leads the matter wherever he pleases.
42. For those who are ignorant of the Mahāyāna, slowness alone is better;
for those lost on the road, lameness is better than speed, which leads to ruin far away.

43. Those who have devotion to the Mahāyāna have gone to the supreme state of the Sugata; even those of our own school [who lack it] go to the underworld, due to wandering in the abyss of the wrong path.

44. Furthermore, when the mind has fully set forth [in its natural state], no further deliberation is applied; for, through the equanimity of the intellect, there is the destruction of the entire cycle of existence.
45. What is the nature of this saṃsāra, which exists as a continuous stream and is characterized by being without beginning or end? Thus do the wise investigate it.
46. From what source and where does the origination and dissolution of this entire universe arise?
[It arises] from its own seed of latent impressions (vāsanā) residing within the storehouse-consciousness (ālayavijñāna).
47. The establishment of the "all-seed" [consciousness] is due to dreaming, fainting, and heedlessness;
and because representation, though ceased, arises again from meditative attainment.
48. The universe, arising from the sense organs and their objects, is designated as "active cognition" (pravṛttijñāna);
being non-different from the storehouse-consciousness (ālayajñāna), it dissolves back into that very same [consciousness].
49. Like water, having displayed various forms through its diverse and flickering waves, it returns in an instant to a state of stillness and sleep.
For that twofold description of it is beyond the scope of reasoning,
just as the echo of a word uttered all at once is beyond the scope of reasoning.
51. Like a magician repeatedly displaying various forms, having seen someone who knows the secret, he abides in his own true nature.
52. Like a chameleon, it displays to the ignorant its own appearance as blue or red;
to the wise, however, it shows various other substances.
53. Its nature is considered to be pure, formless, and stainless;
yet it is indeed impossible for one who lacks awakening to ever know it.
54. For the Buddha does not perceive [reality] as other people do;
indeed, he alone knows that very nature of dependent origination.

55. We, however, merely speak after having inquired through the scriptures, traditions, and so forth, just as those blind from birth [describe] the range of forms belonging to one who possesses sight.
56. For there will indeed come a state through the excellence of the ointment of knowledge, wherein we shall perceive the entire reality with our own selves, just like the Lord of Sages.
57. Whatever is cultivated here by the foolish through a continuous succession, that very thing appears before them, created by the power of cultivation.
58. A limb is afflicted even when covered by garments due to a lack of practice, yet the eyes are not; this is indeed a marvel, for they are struck by intense falls of snow.
59. Due to the power of the practice of meditation, even for a leather-worker whose hide has been kneaded with his hands, the foul odor does not cause excessive distress.
60. Poison, when first consumed by embodied beings, leads only to death;
yet that very same poison, through the practice of habituation, becomes an elixir of immortality in the end.
61. Or from what does the origination of the elements arise? If it is said to be from karma, that is not tenable;
for the elements have no connection with those [karmas], since the latencies of karma reside in the mind.
62. By that very [form], there is a representation of shape: gentle for those who have performed good deeds, but exceedingly terrifying to the predatory—tigers, lions, bears, and serpents.
63. Or else, how could there be the movement of hands, feet, and so forth during other actions, if the elemental constituents were not conceived as having the nature of cognition?
64. If [the body] is moved by wind, from where does that wind come? And from where does that [wind] arise again?
If it is from desire, then you have surely returned to that very same path.
65. How could there be growth from seeds produced as the body, or from the blood and semen of the parents, into the form of a head, hands, and so forth, or into the nature of a tree?
66. Furthermore, why would sound arise from the mouth and also from a drum?
Because its inherent nature (svabhāva) is seen to be absent in each of these individual causes.
67. The flight of birds in the sky, the perception of objects in the darkness, the movement of mice and other creatures within their dwellings, and the swimming of fish in the great oceans;
68. For those who possess enjoyment, both hearing and seeing are functions of the eyes;
for others, these two are contrary, and thus in the cycle of existence they are experienced in various ways.
69. How could those who pierce their enemies through practice have arrows that never miss the mark, even when the location and shape [of the target] are unseen, without the attainment of knowledge?
70. Even that which has been studied but not practiced must undergo study once again;
for what indeed is that which, like a stream, does not flow as a continuous manifestation?
71. Who, if not one who acts through karma, could produce the diversity of mountain-born [forms] and the infinity of the great ocean by means of the transformation of subtle atoms?
Or, having performed [the deed] due to his possession of power, why indeed would he— like a madman—
not destroy it again at the time of its destruction, thereby wasting his own effort?
73. By whom were the powers of magnets and the like to attract iron and other metals, as well as the powers of mantras and medicinal herbs, created?
74. Therefore, all that which is proclaimed through the various manifestations of ignorance and the extensive elaborations of the Ṭaitiṭibhas is merely the outward projection of the mind itself.
75. Or how could the complete meditative cultivation of yogins be successfully accomplished, when the elements possess stable forms and yet their cultivation proceeds in various different ways?
76. But in this way it is logical: this very mind, spreading like oil upon water, appears as the manifold forms of crystal-like delusions.
77. He does not experience wonder at anything that causes wonder in the world, for he has thoroughly contemplated that all things exist within the universal seed-soul (sarvabījaka) without exception.
78. Let these entities remain for now, which have passed beyond verbal description;
but how is their existence determined by you?
79. If, alas, hatred is joined with the mind, why is it without cause? For that very [object] which has that same form is not accepted as the fruit of latent impressions (vāsanā).
80. Or how could cognition, having leaped up, grasp external objects?
Does it exist or not exist initially? If it exists, what is the use of an object?
81. When an object is directly perceived, what is the use of scriptures for its comprehension?
However, regarding that which is not seen, such as the next world and so forth, the word of a reliable authority is followed.
82. However, because it is of interpretable meaning, there is no establishment [of reality] even from the scripture of the authoritative one;
for the teaching of the sense-bases such as form is merely the domain of the mind.
83. Indeed, the sense-faculty is the mind itself arising from its own seed;
once arisen, it takes on the form of the object, and that very [mind] is traditionally called the "object."
84. Thus, by means of the intellect, this division of the mind is conceptualized by the wise, even though the mind is without parts, according to the conventional truth of the world.
85. Here there is no eye, nor form, nor light, nor mental attention;
like a dream, through the delusion of the mind, everything both exists and does not exist.

86. Furthermore, whatever continuous distinction arises from association with good or bad friends through the influence of another's mind, that too is like [the effect of] malevolent spirits or planetary influences.
Death resulting from another's assault is not accepted on the grounds of momentariness;
how much less so in this system where there is neither one who is slain nor one who slays?
88. Just as in the hells, the perception of violent onsets arises here solely for the sake of fear, due to the efficacy of one's own undesirable actions.
89. If phenomena existed by way of their own intrinsic nature exactly as they appear, why would the entire world not be liberated through the vision of reality?

90. For this very reason, in this deluded world, the compassion of the Self-born One is for the sake of dispelling delusion; it would be in vain toward one whose self is already established in its own nature.
91. Lightning, thunder, rain, clouds, wind, and the thunderbolt do not manifest upon the expanse of the sky without being preceded by mere thought.

92. If the arising of entities were established by way of their own nature, then no diversity among them would be seen, despite the difference in people's inclinations; rather, they would appear as one and the same.
93. To one she is a young beloved, to another a woman of middle age;
to one she is stout, to another she is slender, and to yet another she is dark-complexioned.
94. When the mind itself arises in the form of a woman, then what lover, possessed of shame, would desire himself by means of his own self?
95. A wise person should never, like a child, engage in the enjoyment of sense objects, perceiving them at all times as being of the very nature of his own self.
96. Having grasped his own hand with his hand due to the delusion of a dream, the thief is cast aside by others while crying out, "A thief has been caught by me!"
97. Animals [seek food] in dry thickets, while humans have no perception of hunger;
oh, how inconceivable is the course of conceptual constructions, even for yogins!
98. Fire-purified deer eat fire, and mice eat poison;
yet they do not perish even by poisons that bring an end to life.
99. Other beings, such as fish, birds, dogs, and snakes, subsist by means of the mother’s continuous stream of memories, her touch, sleep, and her breath.
100. Due to the variety of karma, the Yakṣa perceives the form of his own abode, crowded with his attendant folk, within the solitary Plakṣa tree; others do not see it.
101. Pretas see a river whose waters are turbid with urine and flowing with pus, whereas humans see it as a flood of clear water and drink from it.
102. This very consciousness, though empty of external objects, proceeds in the form of desired and undesired fruits, being thoroughly permeated by various karmas.
103. Oh, how manifold are the varieties of objects at a single time!
Like the sound of a drum struck by many sticks, they follow after conceptual construction.
104. If the object were [defined as] causal efficiency, then it would not exist even without that [efficiency];
for one person may eat sour food and other substances, yet another's mouth becomes moistened.
105. Even at night, if someone were to eat a cucumber while mocking another and say, "I am eating something sour," would there not be a disturbance in the listener?

106. For indeed, even without an external object, the emission of semen occurs, caused by the attainment of the pleasure of union with a desired woman in a dream; why does it not happen [in the waking state] as well?

107. If it is argued that the apprehension "it exists" occurs even regarding what is seen in a dream due to the power of mental cultivation, this is unreasonable, because one sees the birth of a son from a maiden's womb [in a dream].

108. Because mountains, regions, and the interiors of houses that have been perceived for a long time appear in their distinct forms [within a dream], what is seen in a dream is devoid of objective reality.

109. If it is not admitted that even a manifest action (vijñapti) is devoid of objective reality (anartha) as compared to a non-manifest action, then its resolution indeed falls into the category of grossness.
110. Even that knowledge which belongs to yogins is indeed nothing but ignorance, for it has as its object the minds of others and so forth, just like one's own conviction regarding one's own mind.
111. All conventional knowledge, whether of a wise person or another, functions in exactly the same way regarding both apprehension and verbal designation.
112. From the very first, the vision of emptiness yields a great fruit that is immediately perceived:
he who has attained fearlessness does not tremble, unlike those of other worlds.
113. He who regards both death and life as being like a magical creation—how indeed could fear arise for such a person regarding the self?
114. Even though one considers these three worlds to be nothing but a creation of karma, if one still fears them excessively, alas, a person such as I am is truly ruined.
115. Who would have any fear of the cutting off of a second head or the plucking out of a third eye, since those two do not exist?
116. Thus, by means of the determination of the objects of knowledge, the wise one, even when assailed by the variegated impurities of the substrates, never undergoes defilement; he remains pure.
Like the sky with impure fragments of clouds.
117. What is the use of saying much more here? If anything were to exist [as a self-nature], even a horn growing on the heads of dogs, rabbits, or horses would be seen.
118. Maṇḍūka also was radiant with a mass of matted hair, grey with ashes, wearing a white sacred thread, and carrying a water-pot slung over his shoulder.
119. What is it that a timid person, imagining this or that in the darkness within a house, sees as a non-human being—a manifestation of the forms of his own mind? A child perceives it thus.
120. Having himself assumed such a most formidable yakṣa form, why does the painter not feel fear when seeing it again alone in a secluded place?

121. Due to the conceptualization that "this is a thief," many people experience sudden terror toward a post, and due to the [conceptualization] of a "snake," toward a rope; why do they not [experience it] otherwise?
122. "By means of objects fashioned by his own imagination and craft, the fool is entirely frustrated by unreal objects due to his own transgression."
123. Even though an object is unseen—being equal in being invisible—both at night and during the day, it becomes as if illuminated by the attainment of the word "dawn."
124. Entities such as place, time, and so forth are delusions of dream-consciousness;
even when the path is short, it appears long to one who is weary from traveling.
125. Likewise, for lovers separated from their beloveds, even a single day is equal to a hundred years for men, as it consists of a multitude of passing hours.
126. But by those very persons who have seen reality and have become such as they are, worldly convention is carried out in such a manner, and yet they do not perceive any real object therein.
127. Thus the wise behold this entire universe as a stage for mental construction;
they see it all like a painting, and do not perceive it as having intrinsic nature.

128. Oh, how wondrous, how truly marvelous! Even though it is known through the method of perceiving reality, the mind still harbors delusion regarding the movement across even and uneven, low and high terrains—due to the [traces] inscribed in portions within the sky of the heart throughout beginningless saṃsāra.
By means of false imaginings, this triple world is as if gathered together.
129. For if an entity were truly an entity, how could it ever become a non-entity? Because suchness has a stable nature, it does not undergo any change into something else.
130. He who perceives phenomena as false, through qualities such as name, genus, and so forth—he, struck by perversion, creates a variegated world in a soundless heaven.
131. Therefore, the intrinsic nature of those things whose nature is mind is the absence of intrinsic nature;
he who perceives phenomena otherwise departs from the ultimate truth.
132. If conceptual construction were non-existent and emptiness were existent, then manifestation and disappearance would occur spontaneously and without effort.
133. Conceptual construction does not depart for one who has not understood it;
and without the departure of conceptual construction, emptiness—though established as having a stable nature—is not realized.
134. Indeed, there is no difference whatsoever between these two; it is only conceptualization that has the nature of unreality.
When correctly perceived through its dependent nature, emptiness comes to be.
135. How does one enter into this [reality]? Through the vision of the three natures. When those are seen, the grasping at a solid mass regarding all phenomena ceases.
136. Not seeing them as one and undivided, the three-fold form is clearly perceived;
through the power of the activity of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), that which is imagined appears radiant between the two.
137. Because the imagined object has been abandoned, the dependent nature manifests;
yet, because its true form has not been seen from the beginning, it appears as if it were still in motion.
138. Gradually casting off that manifestation of it, emptiness (śūnyatā) arises again in the heart, radiant as if making that very [emptiness] firm.
139. She too, as unstable as lightning, comes and goes for a moment;
this is entirely due to the constant flux of this very duality that has existed since beginningless time.
140. The pair [of subject and object] sets and follows after it, yet it does not reach the state of non-duality as long as it has not been made motionless within that interval.
141. Having become once more motionless, like the rising of the thousand-rayed sun, she allows no room for the activity of darkness because of its opposition to her.
142. That certain state which is called emptiness (śūnyatā) is incomprehensible to those like me;
it does not, however, follow the worldly convention of nihilism.
143. Its very nature as non-existence is established for the sake of conventional usage;
for when all phenomena are devoid of intrinsic nature, of what could existence or non-existence exist?
144. Just as when it is said, "You must not remember," one remembers that which was forbidden, so too from the word "non-existent" (asat), one arrives at its opposite.
145. The cognition of an object arises from conceptual construction, and conceptual construction also arises from the notion of an object;
since both possess the nature of conceptual construction, what existence could there be, and what non-existence?
146. Even non-existence becomes existence when it is cultivated as its basis in some [context].
If this is accepted, then indeed existence itself would likewise be attained.
147. Thus, existence and non-existence, pleasure and pain, and so forth, are not [inherently] established.
Everything is established through mutual dependence, like the distinction between long and short.
148. What is called "happiness" for a person is merely one's own mental construction based on the subsiding of suffering;
and suffering arises from the loss of happiness—thus, this pair is entirely relative.
149. It should be understood that everything arises through dependence; why is it that others understand even the "one" as being independent?
150. Through the exclusion of others (anyāpoha), a cognition arises—somewhere confused and having an unascertained object—by means of such instruments as instruction.
151. Phonemes, words, sentences, genders, and numbers, as well as the relations between actions and their factors, are non-expressive because they are unreal.
152. Why indeed is a verse not accepted as having five or even three quarters?
Since a sentence depends upon what is to be expressed, it may consist of a *ḍākinī-samaya*.
Why has this world been cast by ancient scholars who considered themselves wise into the narrow strait of grammatical refinement regarding things that ought to be grasped?
154. When one is asked, "Is this the nose? who indeed would point to the head with a crooked hand that turns it clockwise?
155. Like the example of the stone box, he has brought himself to insignificance;
both himself and the world have been reduced by words to a mere heap of noisy frogs.
156. Furthermore, the cognition of one thing by means of another that is unrelated is not logical;
does a sword struck in one place produce an effect in another?
157. By what means, or by whom, is anything brought into being in its inactive form? Or how can an entity be produced by another entity that itself is of the nature of non-existence?
158. The nature of non-existence belongs to an entity at the time of its existence;
it is precisely by virtue of that lack of intrinsic nature that it is described as "past" once its form has ceased.

159. For this very reason, the Protectors—those who are skilled in the nuances of etymological terminology—declare that these are indeed the "great elements" (mahābhūtāni), because they are the foremost among all elements.
160. In a single location, there is neither a hundred nor even as many as a hundred;
nevertheless, when "a hundred" is uttered, an illusion arises in the mind.
161. Whether [the self] is unseen or seen, what is gained by that [realization] for one who has already understood the self?
Whether it be through instruction in speech and so forth, or regarding heaven and the like, or even with respect to a jar.
162. The elephant was Sairāvaṇa’s elephant, and the women were Apsarases;
there was nothing unprecedented in that appearance, for it arose as something already seen and superior.
163. He sees one thing, he speaks another, and even after hearing something else, he adopts yet another;
nevertheless, like a madman, the world does not understand itself.
If one who is insane should think, "I am insane," then he would not truly be insane; for when there is self-awareness of insanity, it is called neither delusion nor intoxication.
165. Since the three worlds appear with forms restricted by place and other factors, they are not indeed erroneous; for this very reason, they are representation-only (vijñapti).
166. "An elephant," its form, and its absence—these are to be understood by the wise as the natures of the imagined and the others, respectively.
167. When there is a manifestation of an object in what is devoid of an object—a basis for the apprehension of a false object—just as in the case of a single elephant created by a magician;
168. For one who perceives in this way, the prior grasping at objects ceases; his mind proceeds as dependent upon that [object] and taking its form.
169. Therefore, that [cognition] which was turbid with forms ceases later on the eighth stage, having become free from latent impressions through the perception of the non-existence of objects.
170. But when the wheel of the mind has ceased, this [being] no longer wanders in saṃsāra;
because of the perfected nature of reality, it revolves as the arising from non-existence.
171. Like a figure in a painting, motionless, devoid of form, and free from longing, he who dwells in the sphere of non-duality neither rejects nor grasps anything at all.

172. By virtue of the empowerment of his former vows, though he is free from conceptual construction, he destroys the darkness of the world throughout the three realms of existence that have no beginning or end, like the orb of the sun.
173. For this very reason, the protectors have declared that for acting persons, whatever fruit of action there is—whether auspicious or inauspicious—is of the nature of conceptual construction.
174. Dharma and adharma, austerity, renunciation, restraint, observance, and self-control;
animals, denizens of hell, ghosts, humans, and the inhabitants of heaven.
The primary elements, the derivative elements, the aggregates, the constituents, the teaching of the Sage,
as well as the Teacher and the disciples— all this is the teaching of conventional reality.
176. This is the means fashioned by the perfectly awakened ones, like a staircase, for leading ordinary people to enter into the ultimate truth.
177. "In the end everything dissolves"—this is merely a consolation for the ignorant. Something else, ineffable and indefinable, shines forth.
178. There, this luminosity of space illuminates emptiness;
it abides in the state devoid of anything, [the state] of both itself and of emptiness.
Seeing nothing at all on this path as it had been described, he seemed to laugh at the entire world— struck down and conquered by the lack of tranquility.
180. Even when reflecting upon his own ancient state, which was solely devoted to the pursuit of that [pleasure], he immediately experiences only shame.
181. If all this is empty, the undertaking of dharmas is purposeless;
for one for whom emptiness is the fulfillment of the goal, truth is indeed purposeless.
182. At that time, even the undertaking of evil is by no means appropriate for him;
indeed, a yogin who perceives emptiness does not clench his fist upon an empty space.
183. But for those who have fallen into conceptual construction, all this is otherwise not so;
for within saṃsāra, the attainment of its fruit occurs through the relationship of cause and effect.
184. But regarding actions performed in a dream, what good or evil is there? A person does not experience the fruit while awake; rather, the entire man experiences it within the dream itself.
185. Upon awakening, because of the knowledge that [the dream] was unreal, the result of the activity in the dream is unreal;
likewise, when that very same knowledge has arisen at the end of everything, the result is in vain.

186. Indeed, the arising and passing away of dreams, firebrands, and magical illusions are seen to be non-different from everything that is observed in the state of causes as well as in the state of effects.
187. Tell me now, what difference is there today between the objects enjoyed on another day and those [enjoyed] in a dream, with respect to the experience of their intrinsic nature?
Whatever arises dependently is by its very nature quiescent,
like the parts of an illusion displayed by a magician after having conjured them together.

189. Just as with garments that have been torn apart in many ways, there is no further distinction whatsoever among the ashes once they have been consumed by the fire of emptiness; so it is with all phenomena, though they appear diverse in manifold ways.
190. Having burned these two worlds known as the sentient beings and the receptacle world, she herself is likewise consumed right there, like a blazing torch.
191. Seeing the three worlds thus consumed by the fire of emptiness, the yogi is not attached anywhere, even while wandering through saṃsāra.
192. When one abides in the void, then that which is subtle arises for him—neither movement, nor conduct, nor investigation, nor even a sphere of experience.
193. Later, abiding in emptiness and devoid of all fuel, it becomes indefinable in nirvana, like a fire when its fuel is exhausted.
Having become thus, detached, indefinable, and stainless,
the knower of yoga neither smokes again nor does he blaze.
195. Not yet burning, it attains tranquility; being tranquil, it reaches subsided calm;
having reached subsided calm, it attains perfect peace; and being perfectly peaceful, it further attains coolness.
196. Having become cooled, he is free from heat; being free from heat, he is said to be without fever.
Without fever, he is passionless, pure, beyond dualities, and free from affliction.
Free from the sense of "mine" and free from the ego, having crossed over the ocean of existence, he is no longer touched by birth; being beyond birth, he does not die.
198. Cast off by birth and death, one attains the immortal state;
having reached that principle, one finds nothing further to be attained.

Furthermore, as he moves about practicing equanimity toward everything, he harbors neither aversion nor attachment toward the sufferings born of saṃsāra, nor toward pleasures which are the causes of suffering.
200. That which is dependent perishes through all [conditions], while that which has its dependence destroyed is forever unimpaired.
The unimpaired attains the Imperishable; that which is not unimpaired, being imperishable, does not perish.
Having attained a firm footing in the imperishable, he does not abide anywhere—
neither in nirvāṇa nor in saṃsāra— by virtue of his mastery and sovereign power.
He is the wielder of the axe, he is the sage, the teacher, the accomplished one, and the Tathāgata;
he is the Sugata whose sovereign power of knowledge thus unfolds.
203. When a fool who is excessively attached to sense objects and whose mind is untrained hears the teaching on emptiness, his heart breaks into two pieces.
204. Through hearing the sublime Dharma, through attending upon virtuous friends, and by virtue of one's spiritual lineage, those who act with diligence achieve entry here.
205. Constantly diligent and applying himself while following this path, one soon realizes the selflessness of all phenomena.
206. Dharma that has not been fully cultivated does not lead to the attainment of the true nature of reality (dharmatā). Can water merely by being seen or heard, even when drunk, ever cut off thirst?
207. Established in virtuous conduct, learned, wise, and having accumulated a store of merit, viewing sense objects as poison, he is free from craving for his body and life.
Whether in a palace or even in a forest, the Bodhisattva, being composed in meditative concentration,
first seeks to ascend to the state of a Buddha by way of selflessness.
209. Having made the welfare of the world his own, the compassionate one made his own body [an instrument] for that purpose;
and he taught the world the cultivation of the three natures of phenomena.

210. Even if one has become a householder, having obtained even a single moment of leisure, one should practice meditation, having assumed the cross-legged posture and fixed the mind immovably upon the tip of the nose.
Placing before him as an object of focus those very enjoyments which are situated nearby— though they are unreal, deceptive, and merely appearing as such to his own mind— [he should practice].
One who is subject to passion does not take as an object that which is a basis for passion, nor does one who possesses hatred take that which is hateful;
likewise, one who is deluded does not again make that which is shrouded in darkness his object.
213. One who is full of passion creates a basis for passion; one who is hateful is oppressed by hatred.
Through the very increase of the afflictions, the deluded person perishes all the more because of his delusion.

214. Because meditative concentration has not yet taken root, he is impaired by conceptual construction; imagining something entirely different through various doors of ruinous distraction, he remains distracted.
Even one who is deluded, by perceiving himself as deluded and contemplating an object that is utterly confused,
falls all the more deeply into blind darkness, wandering like a blind man.
216. A wise person should direct the mind toward an object of focus in a contrary manner;
for even a slight habituation to the afflictions leads to their increase, like the addition of fuel to a flame.

217. Having first practiced such training, one should thereafter strike at the enemies of enlightenment—namely, passion and the other afflictions—which reside within the very heart of the battle, like a hero in the midst of combat.
218. Those who see reality in its entirety have declared that the obscuration of the afflictions and so forth is the [true] obstacle to reality;
therefore, that very [obscuration] must indeed be destroyed with every effort.

219. Thereupon, the yogi should effect a threefold designation through a mind whose nature is [distinguished as] imagined and so forth: [the cognition] which grasps the object, which manifests it, and which is yet empty of the object.
220. One should further contemplate with a wisdom consisting of reflection that has become thoroughly integrated;
one should contemplate the principle of the Perfection of Wisdom as being truly inconceivable.

221. That which I see is not real, and that which I do not see is likewise [not real]; for one blinded by conceptual constructions regarding existing things, it is like the distortion caused by a visual impairment such as cataracts.
222. I see something that is a non-existent thing, imagined and consisting of mere delusion;
though it is without cause, it appears as a cause because I have long been afflicted by signs.
223. Alas, how deluded by false possession is the eye of the world!
It sees a mere tuft of hair upon the mountain peak, yet it does not see the massive mountain itself.
224. Let it be that the world is filled with artisans who pierce hair and pearls, who are exceedingly skilled in their craft and capable of penetrating subtle signs.

225. Everything that is imagined appears as something exceedingly pure in its objective reality to those who perceive objects; it is like the mass of waves tossed and dancing by the wind, appearing to a deer as water.
Yet the water, though present nearby, is not real in the same way as the water in ponds and such.
Generally, that which has become real is grasped effortlessly, even though it has fallen into the category of unreal conceptualization.
One should contemplate in the mind that "it does not exist," regarding signs as having the nature of a dream;
thereupon, one attains the dependent nature which is non-conceptualized.
227. The intrinsic nature appears undefiled, belonging to the stage that is neither fully accomplished nor yet near [to it];
having attained this perfected state, one abides in non-conceptuality.
228. Having perceived even that, the wise person should not enter into another form;
for that [other] is not practiced in reality, because the imagined self is non-existent.
229. If that [object], although perceived there as having the nature of identity with itself, should manifest its own false nature quickly, then one should illustrate it by means of a dream.
230. But when recognized through the mode of dreaming, it does not appear again as having a false nature;
at that moment, it either appears feebly or is paralyzed by its opposite.
231. If one who has thus extracted the essence were to touch the limit of non-existence, then that suchness would be something to be grasped, and it would become an object of reliance.
233. Just as an asura enters his abode through a door smeared with adamantine cement, the yogin enters representation-only (vijñapti), without touching either side.
235. However, the signs to be known here by the yogin who has obtained illumination are those that are infallible for success, like smoke for fire.

236. Because of the removal of this imagined [world] through detachment, like a painting that has been slightly wiped away, even when he has arisen from meditation, he perceives the entire world as dimmed.
Like something decayed, withered, and broken on all sides;
like a deserted village, ruined, without pleasure groves, and without refuge.
238. It produced great agitation in the world, sounding like the cry of a cricket;
it was ownerless, devoid of wealth, and existed as a mere name alone.
But when the nature called "dependent" (paratantra-svabhāva) has been seen,
one then perceives it as if entering within oneself, mounted upon the flow of one's own mind.
240. This [world] is merely an illusion, resembling a magical display;
seeing it entirely as if overwhelmed by darkness, one does not imagine it to be real therein.
241. As if permeated on all sides by the lines of residual latent impressions (*vāsanā*), it is crowded with afflictions (*kleśa*) alone and revolves like a wheel.

242. The cognition arising from deep sleep is both characterized and uncharacterized at that very moment; it is like something seen and then lost, and one perceives it as if it were something indescribable.
243. But when the perfected nature is known, everything is of a single flavor, undivided, without beginning or end, formless, and free from grasping.
Free from agitation, free from exertion, and neither too long nor too round,
it was as stainless as the sky when its darkness has been pierced by the sun.
245. Through the penetration of the equality of dharmas, everything is again equal and the same;
this is the dharma seen by way of conventional truth, but it is not accepted as such from the perspective of ultimate truth.

246. Conceptual construction is called the conventional truth; it is the cause of further conceptual constructions. That very [reality], however, is the ultimate truth, which is the cessation of conceptual construction.
Even that [ultimate reality], according to its designation, remains within the conventional alone;
for the ultimate, as it is his ground, is not such as can be expressed by words.
248. Let there be no reliance upon the conventional; for this very reason, the Sage has no fear. His teaching, though stated repeatedly, shatters [clinging] by means of emptiness as its essence.
Fools, whose minds are attached to conceptual proliferation, remain satisfied with mere mental constructions that have been nurtured for a long time; even now, they continue to nurture them.
250. Regarding the movement toward signs by this wholesome mind, there is no occurrence of conceptual construction; it does not approach anything, nor does it exist anywhere.
251. Having taken recourse to selflessness, the mind becomes as if indifferent, as if sleeping without longing; it rests, as it were, in peace.
252. For those who perceive emptiness, emptiness causes stiffness of the eyes, bowing of the head, and a state of numbness in the mind and mental factors.

253. "I have achieved my purpose from what has already been seen"—thinking thus from the observation of the signs, the hero should not abandon his cultivation [of insight], for there is something further beyond this.
254. This reality cannot be described by anyone as "this is that";
through the practice of this yoga, it is realized by oneself alone.
255. Thus, the state of representation-only (vijñaptimātratā), situated between the two extremes, is perceived;
it reveals the perfection of reality for this entire world.
256. Established thereafter in the perfection of reality, the compassionate son of the Sugata does not practice indifference even toward his own life for the sake of sentient beings.
And what concern can there be for sense-objects, whose functioning has been conquered by sleep,
even when others are enjoying one's own children, wife, and so forth?
258. There is no perturbation of the mind caused by those who are negligent, even if they are exalted;
for one whose mind is equanimous in all circumstances, there is no change of heart whether in prosperity or in adversity.
259. Like an unseasonable cloud suddenly arisen from somewhere in the sky, it reveals itself;
such is that wonderful manifestation.
260. Knowing the proper time, he simultaneously caused both blazing and raining, as well as sinking and emerging like water upon the surface of the earth.
261. The shaking of mountains and other things, as well as their splitting and carrying away, and traveling through the sky by oneself with ease like a royal swan.
Therefore, whatever else is perceived even among external objects,
that which arises through their own inherent nature occurs by this very same path.
264. Seeing nothing at all as a single [independent] entity, the omniscient one sees everything;
for this very reason, although it is differentiated, it is conceived as being of a single nature.
265. When one object is seen from the perspective of ultimate reality, the entire world is seen through that single object;
for when water is drunk at one spot on the bank, [the whole body is satisfied].
The entirety of the ocean would be known.
266. And when [beings] are separated in time, or separated by place and so forth, knowledge does not arise for the Protectors without the vision of emptiness.
267. This external [form], which is a painting produced by the conceptualization of one's own mind, is clear in its configuration; it is radiant, having been cultivated through many lifetimes.
The three worlds are like a variegated painting.
268. All this has been seen by the Protector (Tāyin), who understands the conceptual constructions of its manifold elaborations (prapañca):
as being without intrinsic nature, signless, and imperishable.
And it is merely a mere conceptual construction.
269. Thus, through meditation, those free from passion, no longer longing for the enjoyment of pleasure, gradually [attain] that state which is the desire for the sovereignty of the Lord of Sages.
Those devoted to the welfare of others attain the supreme state.
270. When the division has been explained,
this "Garland of Light" provides a clear arrangement of words for those who do not travel the wrong path.
[— — U] It is that which destroys the darkness of ignorance.
271. Grasping at existence [U - U] cuts off the desire for sense objects;
light in the heart [U - U -UUU - - - U - - U-], the light of knowledge [U - U -UUU - - - U - - U-].
This perfection of wisdom is always a wish-fulfilling gem.
272. Those who assert that conventional reality is a superimposition and that the definitive meaning is [the ultimate], do not accept external objects as being present before them.
The teacher’s closed fist has been opened by the Sugatas.
273. When even you, though having attained the imperishable awakening that is beyond letters, [acted thus],
how much more so for those who have long since lost it?
A false accusation is made by those who act without restraint.
274. Every [entity], when analyzed by an intellect capable of subtle scrutiny, is determined as either belonging to the Buddhist or the non-Buddhist; such is the divider between the two.
If there were not this single teaching of emptiness here, [it would not be so].
275. If the state of omniscience were being postulated, one would have to conceive it as existing without a cause in a self that is distinct [from the Teacher],
or else as having as its cause the Teacher who is subject to momentary destruction.
If emptiness were not both eternal and uniform, [then...]
276. That pride of knowledge regarding the domain of others' minds, which arises in yogins due to the cause of specific supernatural attainments—
one should consider that to be an excessive impurity of darkness (tamas) on their part.
Just as foolish people remain bound by their own nature.
277. Between one who is blind in every respect and one whose eyes are impaired by cataracts, the former alone is far superior;
for he is free from the arrogance of thinking, "I am blind."
One who perceives what is insignificant is like one with cataracts, full of conceit.

278. He who does not recognize his own faults as being of the nature of defects, nor perceives the virtues of the virtuous as they truly are from time immemorial, and treats the spiritual friend with contempt— [he is lost].
How indeed shall he drink the essence of reality?
279. Oh, how people are deceived by others who are experts in the art of painting on the surface of the sky, intent on demonstrating specific objects through their first elaborate displays!
It is elaborated upon by the authors of diverse narratives.
280. For one who sees the footprints of a snake that has gone into the water, who fashions a garland of sky-flowers,
and who weaves a cloth without thread—
How indeed does shame not arise in the world?
281. Even he who approaches this teaching of the Lord of Munis merely out of a desire for censure, and not out of devotion—
just as one might approach a bitter substance after having encountered something very sweet— [attains this result].
Who indeed would follow a word spoken by another?
